question: Alec controls [Elspeth Conquers Death] and puts the third lore counter it. With the triggered ability, they target [Eternal Witness] in their graveyard. When Eternal Witness returns to the battlefield, can it target Elspeth Conquers Death with its trigger?
answer:
Yes — by the time targets are chosen for Eternal Witness's triggered ability, Elspeth Conquers Death is already in Alec's graveyard, so it's a legal target and can be returned to Alec's hand.

Why: Chapter III of Elspeth Conquers Death resolves and returns Eternal Witness to the battlefield. Because the number of lore counters is now at least the greatest chapter number, Alec sacrifices Elspeth Conquers Death as a state-based action as soon as that chapter ability leaves the stack, and this doesn't use the stack [Elspeth Conquers Death ruling #11]. State-based actions and putting triggered abilities on the stack both happen before a player next receives priority, and a triggered ability's targets are chosen as the ability is put on the stack [115.1d]. So when Eternal Witness's "When this creature enters, you may return target card from your graveyard to your hand" ability is put on the stack, Elspeth Conquers Death is already a card in Alec's graveyard and may be chosen as the target.

This is the same principle as Eternal Witness's own ruling that its ability can target a card that reaches your graveyard as the spell/ability that put Eternal Witness onto the battlefield finishes resolving [Eternal Witness ruling #0].

Note that Eternal Witness's ability says "you may," so Alec still chooses whether to return Elspeth Conquers Death on resolution; the target must still be chosen up front, though.

Nothing here depends on player count — the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Yes.

question: Autumn attacks with [Robber of the Rich], exiling [Light Up the Stage] from Nehemiah's library. Can Autumn pay Light Up the Stage's Spectacle cost with only {C}?
answer:
Yes — assuming an opponent has lost life this turn, Autumn can pay Light Up the Stage's spectacle cost of {R} using one {C} (colorless) mana, because Robber of the Rich says "you may spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell."

How it works:
- Spectacle is a static ability functioning on the stack meaning "You may pay [cost] rather than pay this spell's mana cost if an opponent lost life this turn" [702.137a]. Light Up the Stage's spectacle cost is {R}, a single red mana — not generic, so ordinarily colorless mana couldn't pay it.
- Robber of the Rich's own text grants an "as though" permission. Under [609.4b], an effect letting you spend mana as though it were mana of any color affects only how you may pay a cost; it doesn't change the cost and doesn't change what mana was actually spent. So the cost is still {R}, but your {C} is legal payment for it. This card text is what overrides the normal color requirement.
- The permission applies to the spectacle cost as well as the normal mana cost, since Robber of the Rich says you may spend mana that way "to cast that spell," and casting for an alternative cost is still casting the spell [702.137a, 601.2h].

Two conditions Autumn still must satisfy:
1. An opponent must have lost life this turn. Attacking with Robber of the Rich does not by itself cause life loss; if Robber of the Rich (or anything else) dealt damage to an opponent, that counts, since damage dealt to a player causes that player to lose that much life [Light Up the Stage ruling #4]. Spectacle only cares that life was lost at some point this turn, even if it was later gained back [Light Up the Stage ruling #6].
2. Timing. Neither spectacle nor Robber of the Rich changes when a spell can be cast [Light Up the Stage ruling #8, Robber of the Rich ruling #6]. Light Up the Stage is a sorcery, so Autumn must cast it during one of their own main phases with an empty stack — in practice, the postcombat main phase of the turn they attacked with the Rogue. Autumn may cast it even if Robber of the Rich has left combat or the battlefield [Robber of the Rich ruling #3, ruling #5], as long as Autumn attacked with a Rogue that turn.

Also note the total cost is locked in as {R} (paid with {C} via the "as though" effect) plus any cost increases, then reductions [Light Up the Stage ruling #5, 601.2h]; the mana value of Light Up the Stage stays 3.

Multiplayer note: in a game with more than two players, Nehemiah is the defending player for Robber of the Rich's trigger (or the controller of the planeswalker being attacked) [Robber of the Rich ruling #9], and the life loss for spectacle can come from any opponent, even one who has since left the game [Light Up the Stage ruling #3]. The answer is otherwise identical with two players.

question: Nico controls [Urza's Saga] with two lore counters on it. Alexzander uses [Jinx] to change its land type. What happens?
answer:
Direct answer: Urza's Saga becomes the basic land type Alexzander chose (say, an Island), losing its chapter abilities, and per Urza's Saga ruling #1 it is then immediately sacrificed by Nico — even though it never got to chapter III.

Why: Jinx says "Target land becomes the basic land type of your choice until end of turn." Setting a land's subtype to a basic land type makes it lose its old land type and all abilities generated from its rules text, and it gains the mana ability of the new basic type [305.7]. Urza's Saga's chapter symbols are keyword abilities representing triggered abilities printed in its text box [107.15a][714.2b], so they are rules-text abilities and are gone. Card types and supertypes are untouched by a subtype change [305.7][205.4b], so it remains an enchantment/land object that is still a Saga.

Urza's Saga ruling #1 addresses exactly this situation (it names Blood Moon as the example): "If Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, perhaps due to a card like Blood Moon, it will immediately be sacrificed." Note that the state-based action as worded in [704.5s]/[714.4] speaks of a Saga "with one or more chapter abilities"; the card-specific ruling is what governs here, and it says the sacrifice happens.

Abilities Urza's Saga already gained from its resolved chapter I and chapter II abilities ("{T}: Add {C}" and the {2}, {T} Construct-token ability) were granted by other effects, and [305.7] explicitly does not remove abilities granted to the land by other effects — but that hardly matters, since the permanent is sacrificed right away. Also, with no chapter abilities it would receive no lore counter at the start of Nico's next precombat main phase [505.4][703.4f][714.3c].

Timing note: Jinx's effect only lasts until end of turn, but the sacrifice is a state-based action checked immediately, so Nico can't wait for the effect to wear off. If instead you read the question as Jinx resolving at a moment when a chapter ability of Urza's Saga is already on the stack, the sacrifice would be delayed until that ability leaves the stack [704.5s][714.4].

This works the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

question: Ada controls [Ethersworn Canonist]. They want to suspend [Shade of Trokair] and then cast [Divination]. Can they?
answer:
Yes — assuming Ada hasn't cast any nonartifact spell yet this turn, they can suspend Shade of Trokair and then cast Divination.

Why: Exiling a card with suspend is a special action, not casting a spell ([116.2f], [702.62a], [Shade of Trokair ruling #7]). Ethersworn Canonist only restricts *casting* additional nonartifact spells, so paying {W} to exile Shade of Trokair with three time counters doesn't count against the Canonist's limit and isn't itself blocked by it.

The one requirement is that Ada must be able to *begin to cast* Shade of Trokair at that moment ([116.2f], [702.62c], [601.3], [Shade of Trokair ruling #2]). Since Shade of Trokair is a creature card, that means during Ada's main phase with an empty stack and priority ([117.1a]). Because Ada hasn't cast a nonartifact spell yet, Ethersworn Canonist isn't prohibiting them, so the suspend action is legal. Afterward, casting Divination ({2}{U}) is their one permitted nonartifact spell for the turn ([Ethersworn Canonist ruling #1]).

Order matters: if Ada casts Divination first, Ethersworn Canonist then prohibits them from casting Shade of Trokair, so they could no longer take the suspend special action that turn ([702.62c], [601.3]). Note also that when the last time counter is later removed, casting Shade of Trokair from exile *is* casting a nonartifact spell, so Ethersworn Canonist could prevent that on the turn it resolves if Ada has already cast a nonartifact spell that turn.

This works the same at any table size; Ethersworn Canonist applies per player, so each opponent independently gets their own one nonartifact spell per turn.

question: Asa controls an [Inventors' Fair], a [Krark-Clan Ironworks], and two [Piston Sledge]. They want to activate the last ability of Inventors' Fair and sacrifice a Piston Sledge to help pay the cost. Is this legal?
answer:
Yes, it's legal — but only indirectly, by sacrificing a Piston Sledge to Krark-Clan Ironworks' mana ability and using the {C}{C} it produces toward Inventors' Fair's {4}.

Details:

1. Inventors' Fair's last ability costs {4}, {T}, Sacrifice Inventors' Fair, and can only be activated if Asa controls three or more artifacts. Asa controls exactly three artifacts (Krark-Clan Ironworks and the two Piston Sledge) — Inventors' Fair itself is a land, not an artifact. The artifact count is checked only as the ability is activated, not again on resolution [Inventors' Fair ruling #2].

2. There is no "sacrifice an artifact" component in Inventors' Fair's cost, so Asa cannot hand over a Piston Sledge directly as payment. Instead, while paying the total cost, Asa may activate Krark-Clan Ironworks' mana ability ("Sacrifice an artifact: Add {C}{C}"), sacrificing a Piston Sledge. Rule 605.3a expressly allows activating a mana ability in the middle of activating an ability that requires a mana payment.

3. Each payment applies to only one cost (rule 118.10): sacrificing the Piston Sledge pays Krark-Clan Ironworks' activation cost, and the resulting {C}{C} pays part of Inventors' Fair's cost. That's fine — they're two different costs.

4. {4} is generic mana, payable with any mana including colorless, so {C}{C} covers two of it; Asa still needs {2} more from other sources (Inventors' Fair's own {T}: Add {C} is unavailable, since the {T} is being used for the ability's cost). Once Asa has enough mana in their mana pool, they pay all costs in any order, and partial payments aren't allowed (rules 601.2h, 118.3).

5. Losing a Piston Sledge during payment doesn't retroactively invalidate the activation, since the three-artifact condition was already satisfied and checked at activation [Inventors' Fair ruling #2].

Note also that activating mana abilities isn't mandatory (rule 118.3c) — Asa chooses to do this. Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Amare controls [Psychogenic Probe] and casts [Pain], targeting Nico. They discard a [Progenitus]. Does Psychogenic Probe trigger?
answer:
Yes — Psychogenic Probe triggers and deals 2 damage to Nico.

Why: Pain resolves and Nico discards a card. Progenitus has a replacement ability reading "If Progenitus would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, reveal Progenitus and shuffle it into its owner's library instead." So instead of going to the graveyard, Progenitus is revealed and shuffled into Nico's library. That shuffle is caused by an ability (Progenitus's own replacement ability, set in motion by the spell Pain), which is exactly what Psychogenic Probe looks for: "Whenever a spell or ability causes a player to shuffle their library, this artifact deals 2 damage to that player." The player who shuffled is Nico, so Nico takes the 2 damage, even though Amare controls Psychogenic Probe.

The trigger event genuinely occurs, so the ability triggers normally (an ability triggers whenever a game event matches its trigger event) [603.2g]. Note also that Psychogenic Probe's ability triggers even if the library being shuffled is empty [Psychogenic Probe ruling #0] — not relevant here, but it shows the trigger cares only that a shuffle happened.

Practical note: Psychogenic Probe's ability goes on the stack after Pain finishes resolving and resolves separately, so Nico takes the 2 damage shortly after the discard. Progenitus's protection from everything doesn't help here — the discard doesn't target Progenitus, and the damage is dealt to Nico, not to Progenitus [Progenitus ruling #1]. Also, only one card was discarded: a split card like Pain // Suffering is a single card, and Progenitus is a single card too [Pain // Suffering ruling #0].

This works the same regardless of the number of players; the damage always goes to whichever player actually shuffled — here Nico.

question: Albert controls [Doubling Season] and [Pir, Imaginative Rascal] and activates the +1 ability of [Ajani, Mentor of Heroes]. How many loyalty counters does it gain?
answer:
Ajani, Mentor of Heroes gains exactly 1 loyalty counter — neither Doubling Season nor Pir, Imaginative Rascal applies.

Why: the "+1" in Ajani, Mentor of Heroes' ability is a cost you pay to activate the loyalty ability (rule 606.5 treats loyalty additions/removals as costs), not something an effect does. Doubling Season and Pir, Imaginative Rascal are replacement effects that only apply to counters an *effect* would put on a permanent, so counters put on as a cost aren't modified [Doubling Season ruling #4].

The +1/+1 counters from the ability's resolution are a different story: those are put on by an effect, so both replacement effects apply and Albert (the affected permanents' controller) chooses the order for each creature (rule 616.1g). For a creature receiving n of the distributed counters: applying Pir, Imaginative Rascal first gives (n+1) then doubling gives 2n+2; applying Doubling Season first gives 2n then Pir, Imaginative Rascal gives 2n+1. So putting all three counters on one creature and applying Pir, Imaginative Rascal first yields 8 counters, which is the maximum.

Note you announce the distribution (each target getting at least one counter) as you activate the ability [Ajani, Mentor of Heroes ruling #1]. Player count doesn't matter here — this works identically in a two-player or multiplayer game; only Albert's own choices are involved. (Pir, Imaginative Rascal's "your team" wording can extend to a teammate's permanents in team formats.)

question: Aminah casts a [Show and Tell]. As it resolves, Aminah chooses to put a [Haru-Onna] onto the battlefield and Nico chooses to put a [Domestication] onto the battlefield enchanting Haru-Onna. Who controls the enters-the-battlefield ability of Haru-Onna?
answer:
Nico controls Haru-Onna's enters-the-battlefield triggered ability, so Nico draws the card.

Why: Show and Tell puts all the chosen cards onto the battlefield simultaneously, after every player has chosen ([Show and Tell ruling #2]), with any choices (such as what Domestication enchants) made after all players choose ([Show and Tell ruling #0]). So Haru-Onna and Domestication arrive at the same time, with Domestication already attached to Haru-Onna. Haru-Onna enters under Aminah's control by default (110.2a, 302.2), but Domestication's static ability "You control enchanted creature" is a control-changing effect applied in layer 2 (613.1b), and Nico controls Domestication itself — an Aura's controller is separate from the enchanted permanent's controller (303.4e). Because that continuous effect is already applying the moment both permanents are on the battlefield, Haru-Onna is under Nico's control at the time its "When this creature enters" ability triggers.

The controller of a triggered ability is the player who controlled the ability's source when it triggered (113.8, 603.3a, and 109.4b for the window before it's put on the stack). Since Nico controlled Haru-Onna at that moment, Nico controls the trigger, puts it on the stack, and "draw a card" refers to Nico.

Timing note: this assumes the standard Show and Tell resolution, where both permanents enter simultaneously and Domestication's attachment is set as it enters. If instead Domestication somehow became attached to Haru-Onna only after Haru-Onna was already on the battlefield (a later Aura, for example), the enters-the-battlefield ability would already have triggered under Aminah's control, and Aminah would draw.

Multiplayer: this works the same regardless of the number of players — the only difference is the order of choosing (active player first, then others in turn order, per [Show and Tell ruling #2]); the control determination is unchanged.

question:
Amani controls a [Founding the Third Path], and its third ability is resolving. Amani chooses to cast a [Fatal Push] from their graveyard. Amani currently does not have Revolt.
Can Amani choose to target [Skyhunter Patrol] with Fatal Push? Will Skyhunter Patrol be destroyed by Fatal Push?
answer:
Yes, Amani can legally choose Skyhunter Patrol as the target, but Skyhunter Patrol will not be destroyed.

Targeting: Fatal Push says "Destroy target creature if it has mana value 2 or less." The mana value restriction is not part of the targeting requirement — Fatal Push can target any creature, even one with mana value 5 or greater, and the creature's mana value is checked only as Fatal Push resolves ([Fatal Push ruling #3]). Skyhunter Patrol is a permanent on the battlefield, so it's a legal target ([115.2]).

Resolution: When Fatal Push resolves, Skyhunter Patrol is still a legal target, so Fatal Push resolves ([608.2b]). Skyhunter Patrol's mana cost is {2}{W}{W}, so its mana value is 4. Since Amani has not satisfied revolt (no permanent left the battlefield under Amani's control this turn), only the "mana value 2 or less" clause applies, and 4 is not 2 or less. Fatal Push resolves but does nothing; Skyhunter Patrol survives. If a permanent had left the battlefield under Amani's control earlier this turn — for any reason, including a sacrificed permanent or a token ([Fatal Push ruling #0], [Fatal Push ruling #2]) — revolt would be satisfied and Skyhunter Patrol (mana value 4) would be destroyed.

One mechanical note on the cast itself: Founding the Third Path's chapter III exiles the instant or sorcery card from Amani's graveyard, copies it, and Amani may cast the copy — Amani must pay all costs for that copy (here {B}), and must cast it right then as the ability resolves, not later ([Founding the Third Path ruling #2]).

If Skyhunter Patrol is controlled by an opponent, casting Fatal Push targeting it is a crime ([Crime], [700.13]). That's true whether the game is two-player or multiplayer; the answer above is otherwise unchanged by player count, since Fatal Push targets a single creature regardless of who controls it.

question: Ari controls [Bludgeon Brawl] and [Soldevi Digger]. They cast [Titania's Song]. Once it resolves, what are the characteristics of Soldevi Digger?
answer:
Soldevi Digger becomes a 2/2 colorless artifact creature with no abilities, and it is no longer an Equipment.

Details:

- Titania's Song makes each noncreature artifact lose all abilities and become an artifact creature with power and toughness each equal to its mana value. Soldevi Digger's mana cost is {2} (two generic mana), so its mana value is 2 — it is a 2/2.
- Its own activated ability, "{2}: Put the top card of your graveyard on the bottom of your library," is gone (abilities are removed in the ability-modifying layer, per the layer system described in 613.6).
- Because Soldevi Digger is now a creature, Bludgeon Brawl (which only affects each noncreature, non-Equipment artifact) no longer applies to it. Per [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #2], it stops being an Equipment and becomes unattached from any creature it was attached to, while remaining on the battlefield. It therefore also loses the granted equip {X} ability and the "Equipped creature gets +X/+0" ability. (Also relevant: [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #3] — an Equipment that's also a creature can't be equipped to anything.)
- Unchanged characteristics: name Soldevi Digger, mana cost {2}, colorless (no colored mana symbols in its cost), card type artifact (now artifact creature), no creature subtypes.
- Practical note per [Titania's Song ruling #0]: Soldevi Digger can only attack or use {T} abilities if Ari has controlled it continuously since the beginning of their most recent turn.
- If Titania's Song later leaves the battlefield, its own text says the effect continues until end of turn, so Soldevi Digger stays a 2/2 ability-less creature (and stays non-Equipment) until the turn ends.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Audrey casts [Enlarge] targeting [Goblin Piker], and then attacks with the Goblin Piker. Nico blocks it with a [Baron Sengir], which has gained infect due to their [Grafted Exoskeleton] and indestructible due to their [Withstand Death]. What happens at the end of the turn?
answer:
At end of turn, Goblin Piker dies and Baron Sengir survives.

What happens during combat first: Enlarge makes Goblin Piker 9/8 with trample, and Grafted Exoskeleton makes Baron Sengir a 7/7 with infect while Withstand Death makes it indestructible.

- Goblin Piker deals 9 combat damage: at least 7 (lethal) to Baron Sengir, and the excess can trample through to Nico. Baron Sengir is indestructible, so the 7 damage marked on it destroys nothing. Goblin Piker doesn't have infect, so damage to Nico is ordinary life loss, not poison counters.
- Baron Sengir, having infect, deals its 7 damage to Goblin Piker not as marked damage but as seven -1/-1 counters [702.90c]. In layer 7, Goblin Piker is base 2/1, +7/+7 from Enlarge, and -7/-7 from the counters = 2/1 [613.1g]. Toughness is above 0, so Goblin Piker survives combat.

Then, in the cleanup step, all damage marked on permanents is removed and all "until end of turn" effects end simultaneously [514.2]. Enlarge's +7/+7 (and its trample) go away, and Withstand Death's indestructible goes away. The seven -1/-1 counters from Baron Sengir's infect damage do not go away — they stay indefinitely [Grafted Exoskeleton ruling #6]. So Goblin Piker is now 2/1 with seven -1/-1 counters, i.e. -5/-6. As a state-based action, a creature with toughness 0 or less is put into its owner's graveyard, and regeneration can't save it [704.5f].

Baron Sengir loses indestructible at the same moment its marked damage is removed, so it is in no danger and remains a 7/7 while equipped with Grafted Exoskeleton. Because Goblin Piker was dealt damage by Baron Sengir this turn and then dies, Baron Sengir's triggered ability triggers and will put a +2/+2 counter on it once it resolves.

Timing note: I'm assuming Enlarge was cast and resolved before blockers and combat damage, as described. If instead Goblin Piker somehow never received Baron Sengir's infect damage, it would keep no -1/-1 counters and would simply shrink back to 2/1 and live.

With more than two players, nothing here changes except that only the defending player (Nico) takes the trample damage.

question: Niko has a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] in their graveyard with 2 +1/+1 counters on it. Ashley controls [Containment Priest], and casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Niko. What happens?
answer:
Honest answer: the Comprehensive Rules excerpts I was given do not cover this interaction, so I can't ground it in a numbered rule.

The provided rules text is about unrelated topics — blight (701.68b), where abilities function (113.6m), scavenge (702.97a), layers (613.6), replacement effects that modify how a permanent enters and cause library exiling (614.13c), shuffling (701.24g), amass (701.47a/c/d), embalm (702.128a), state-based actions and last known information (704.8), graft (702.58b), and Walker tokens. None of these address manifesting, the "exile it instead" replacement of a creature entering the battlefield, or whether counters stay on a card that changes zones.

What I can say from the card text and rulings supplied (which I flagged before): Ghastly Conscription manifests the exiled creature cards, manifesting is not casting, and Containment Priest ruling #1 states its ability only spares creatures that were cast — so Skullbriar, the Walking Grave would be exiled instead of entering the battlefield. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own printed text ("Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library") plus Skullbriar, the Walking Grave rulings #1, #2 and #5 indicate it keeps its two +1/+1 counters in exile. If Containment Priest instead entered at the same time as the manifested cards, Containment Priest ruling #2 says it wouldn't affect them.

What's missing to settle it from the rules text: the rules on manifest, on replacement effects that exile a permanent as it would enter the battlefield, and on counters ceasing to exist when an object changes zones.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.122.2: Counters on an object are not retained if that object moves from one zone to another. The counters are not “removed”; they simply cease to exist. See rule 400.7.
gold_text.406.7: If an object in the exile zone becomes exiled, it doesn’t change zones, but it becomes a new object that has just been exiled.
gold_text.701.40a: Manifest To manifest a card, turn it face down. It becomes a 2/2 face-down creature card with no text, no name, no subtypes, and no mana cost. Put that card onto the battlefield face down. That permanent is a manifested permanent for as long as it remains face down. The effect defining its characteristics works while the card is face down and ends when it’s turned face up.

answer_gold: In order for counters to remain on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, it needs to have that ability immediately before it changes zones. It did have that ability in the graveyard, so it is exiled face down with the +1/+1 counters remaining on it during that change. It then attempts to enter the battlefield, but remains in exile instead due to Containment Priest. Since it becomes a new object, it will be face-up in exile. However it didn't change zones, so the counters will remain on it in exile.

question: Ashley controls [Skill Borrower] and [Sensei's Divining Top]. The top card of their library is a [Putrid Leech]. Ashley activates Skill Borrower's ability, then activates Sensei's Divining Top's first ability, choosing to put Putrid Leech second from the top. Then they activate Sensei's Divining Top again, putting Putrid Leech back on top. Can Ashley activate Skill Borrower's ability again?
answer:
Yes — Ashley can activate the "Pay 2 life: This creature gets +2/+2 until end of turn" ability again.

Why: Skill Borrower says "Play with the top card of your library revealed" and grants it all activated abilities of that top card. When Sensei's Divining Top's first ability put Putrid Leech second from the top, Putrid Leech stopped being revealed; when it came back to the top after the second activation of Sensei's Divining Top's first ability, it became a *new object* [401.6].

Because the granted ability now comes from a new object, Skill Borrower has acquired a new, separate activated ability. A use restriction like "Activate only once each turn" that Skill Borrower picks up from another object applies only to that ability as acquired from that object, and not to other, identically worded abilities [602.5c]. So the earlier activation this turn doesn't lock out the freshly granted copy.

Timing note/assumption: I'm assuming each activation fully resolved before the next was started, and that Putrid Leech genuinely left the top of the library (was second from the top) in between. If Ashley had looked with Sensei's Divining Top's first ability and left Putrid Leech on top the whole time, it would remain the same object, the same ability would still be restricted, and the second activation would be illegal — a player can't begin to activate an ability that's prohibited from being activated [602.5]. Also note that while the top card changes during the casting/activation of something, the new top card isn't revealed until that process finishes [401.5], and if the top card changes while you're activating a gained ability, that ability is still activated and resolves normally [Skill Borrower ruling #4].

This answer doesn't depend on player count; it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Noah controls a [Mons's Goblin Raiders] enchanted with a [Spider Umbra]. Alexandra casts [Yamabushi's Flame], targeting Mons's Goblin Raiders. What happens?
answer:
Mons's Goblin Raiders survives and Spider Umbra is destroyed. Yamabushi's Flame is not exiling anything.

Details: Spider Umbra makes Mons's Goblin Raiders a 2/2 with reach and grants umbra armor, which means "If enchanted creature would be destroyed, instead remove all damage marked on it and destroy this Aura" [702.89a]. Yamabushi's Flame deals 3 damage to Mons's Goblin Raiders — lethal for a 2/2 — so the game's lethal-damage state-based action would destroy it; umbra armor replaces that destruction instead: all damage is removed from Mons's Goblin Raiders and Spider Umbra goes to Noah's graveyard [Spider Umbra ruling #4].

Because Mons's Goblin Raiders is never destroyed, it never "would die" from the damage, so Yamabushi's Flame's exile-replacement clause has nothing to replace. Note the ruling that when lethal damage (rather than a "destroy" instruction) is involved, it's the game rules on lethal damage that cause the Aura to be destroyed, not Yamabushi's Flame itself [Spider Umbra ruling #0].

After Spider Umbra leaves the battlefield, Mons's Goblin Raiders is a 1/1 again with no damage marked on it (umbra armor already removed the damage), so it isn't destroyed a second time. Its toughness isn't 0 or less, so the toughness state-based action doesn't apply either [704.5f]. Umbra armor also isn't regeneration, so Mons's Goblin Raiders isn't tapped or removed from combat [Spider Umbra ruling #3].

This works the same regardless of how many players are at the table; nothing here depends on player count.

Spider Umbra is destroyed and Mons's Goblin Raiders remains on the battlefield.

The "move to the graveyard" event is a part of the "destroy" event, so the umbra armor replacement effect must apply first. Once that effect has been applied, the creature is no longer about to die, so there are no more effects to apply.

If the Mons's Goblin Raiders would die later in the turn, the Yamabushi's Flame's replacement effect will apply at that time and cause it to move to exile instead of the graveyard.

question: At the beginning of the game, Alex announced [Kaheera, the Orphanguard] as their companion. During the game, Alex cast [Carrion Grub] from their sideboard with [Wish]. Later, Alex restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?
answer:
Short answer: Carrion Grub becomes part of Alex's library for the new game, and because of that Alex's starting deck for the new game no longer meets Kaheera, the Orphanguard's companion requirement, so Kaheera, the Orphanguard can't be a legal companion in the restarted game.

Details:

1. Restarting. Karn Liberated's −14 ability immediately ends the current game (no one wins, loses, or draws) and all players still in it begin a new game following the normal pregame procedure of rule 103, except as modified by rule 727 [727.1], [104.6], [Karn Liberated ruling #12], [Karn Liberated ruling #9].

2. Carrion Grub. Every Magic card involved in the ended game is involved in the new game, even if it wasn't originally part of it; ownership doesn't change, and a card brought in from outside the game ends up in its owner's library when the new game begins [727.2]. Carrion Grub was brought in from outside the game with Wish [Wish ruling #0], so Carrion Grub is shuffled into Alex's library as part of Alex's deck for the new game. (Only non-Aura permanent cards exiled with Karn Liberated's first two abilities stay in exile [727.5], [727.5a], [Karn Liberated ruling #6]; Carrion Grub wasn't exiled that way. Also, players may not shift cards between deck and sideboard before the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #5].)

3. Kaheera, the Orphanguard. Kaheera, the Orphanguard is revealed from outside the game and stays outside the game until Alex pays {3} to put it into their hand [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #0], [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #10], [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #14]. Assuming Alex never paid {3} (the wording of the question suggests Kaheera, the Orphanguard was still outside the game), the new game uses the normal pregame procedure, where a companion is revealed before shuffling and only if the starting deck — the deck after setting aside sideboard cards — meets the requirement [702.139b], [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #0], [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #2]. Carrion Grub is an Insect creature card, not a Cat, Elemental, Nightmare, Dinosaur, or Beast, and it is now in Alex's deck rather than the sideboard, so Kaheera, the Orphanguard cannot legally be revealed as companion for the restarted game. Note Kaheera, the Orphanguard's abilities do nothing while it is outside the game anyway [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #4].

Alternate timing/assumption: if Alex had already paid {3} to put Kaheera, the Orphanguard into their hand before the restart, Kaheera, the Orphanguard was in the game [702.139c], [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #11], so under rule 727.2 it too simply becomes part of Alex's library in the new game and there is no companion at all.

4. Finishing the restart. After the pregame procedure but before the first untap step, Karn Liberated's ability finishes resolving and any cards it left in exile are put onto the battlefield under Alex's control; triggered abilities wait for the first upkeep step [727.4], [Karn Liberated ruling #4], [Karn Liberated ruling #2].

Player count: this works the same with two players or more. In multiplayer, all players still in the game when it restarted are involved regardless of range of influence [727.7], but anyone who had already left the game before the restart is not in the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #11].
